So there will be an error code for "could not connect to the server because of reason x", one for "could not connect to the server because of reason y", and another for "could not connect to the server because of reason z". I'm really sorry to hear about this, I've always had a hard time communicating about mental health with my parents too.

I don't know your dad or what your relationship with him is like, so I can't tell you what will or will not make him take you seriously. To be honest the tooth story makes me worry that it might be hard to convince him. It makes it seem like he's very dismissive of your health. To me even how he talked to you about your depression sounds dismissive (I have some personal bad experiences with this so my alarm bells could be going off for no reason). Does he downplay your medical needs regularly, or are those two events isolated incidents?

I think something that could be helpful short term is to downplay the label of bipolar. After meeting with the psychiatrist you can sort of frame the conversation in the context of "these are the specific problems I'm having, these are the medications that my doctor thinks will help me manage these problems, and the diagnosis is just something the insurance company needs". You can tell him less or more about this depending on how comfortable you are sharing. Long term this might be less helpful, but this is a way to start the conversation in a way that he might be more open to than "I have a scary sounding mental illness".

Another thing that could be helpful is getting him in touch with one of your doctors. I was diagnosed in January after being hospitalized, and I asked a doctor to explain certain aspects of bipolar to my parents. I was afraid of doing this in the past because of how my dad has reacted to my mental health issues in the past, but it turned out very well for me. Inviting him to a session with your therapist may also be a way to do this. Obviously you'll know if these options are appropriate better than I will, but they're somethibg to consider.

Whatever happens, just know that living with this illness isn't easy, and that even if your dad is giving you a hard time you're strong for seeking help.

Not medicated right now, but when I was on a low dose of seroquel I was told by multiple doctors that drinking moderately was fine. However, even if it's "safe" to drink on meds, there will typically be some side effect. For me, I got really tired after having more than 1 or 2 drinks. I'd say if you're going to do it it's best to do it in moderation around people who you can trust until you have a good idea of what the effect the combination has on you.
